tweets.text: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

“Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). Over the last two weeks, both the U.S. Government and Anthropic took significant actions that demonstrated their power to control access to AI by restricting what others can do with frontier models. This has been one of those moments that, once seen, will be hard to unsee, and it is significantly accelerating many businesses’ and nation states’ efforts to ensure reliable access to AI that no one else can terminate. Anthropic first released Claude Fable 5, a version of its Mythos model with additional guardrails, including some restrictions that seem well justified on safety grounds (such as limitations on applying it to hacking, bioweapons, and so forth). However, it also restricted developers’ ability to use it to build competing LLM technology. This move was concerning, given that the whole AI community, including Anthropic, has benefitted tremendously from open research — indeed, the AI revolution was kicked off by my former team (Google Brain) freely publishing the Transformers paper! Imagine if Microsoft’s terms of use barred anyone from using their tools to build competitive software, or if Google barred using it to search for information to work on competing search engines. Anthropic’s argument that it was unsafe for others to be able to make advances in AI also rang hollow. Initially, Anthropic silently degraded Fable 5’s performance for users detected to be working on LLM research through invisible interventions that weakened the model’s outputs without notifying the user. After significant backlash, it walked back this decision and decided to be transparent when it did this, but it still refuses to use its latest capabilities to help AI researchers. This move represents a raw demonstration of power by Anthropic. It has used “safety” arguments to hinder potential competitors. Platforms succeed when they are viewed as stable, reliable partners that one can build on. The sudden rule changes by Anthropic (including a mandatory 30 day data retention policy for Fable usage) have made developers wonder about the stability of building on any one proprietary LLM provider, not just Anthropic. The U.S. Government then shortly followed with an even greater demonstration of power. It used the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate technologies that may be national security threats to restrict exports of Mythos and Fable, requiring a license for use by any foreign national, whether inside or outside of the U.S., including employees of Anthropic. This led Anthropic to disable access to Fable to all users worldwide. Sam Altman pointed out, referring to Anthropic, “It is clearly incredible marketing to say, ‘We have built a bomb, we are about to drop it on your head. We will sell you a bomb shelter for $100 million.’” But when one engages in this type of fear-based marketing, it increases the odds that the U.S. Government will agree with you and slap export controls on the bomb you say you have built. To be clear, I don't think Anthropic has built anything like a bomb, and I don't think export controls on Fable are appropriate. However, following the U.S. Government making this move, many nations, including U.S. allies, saw how the U.S. can suddenly yank their access to AI models. In many capitals around the world, this has spurred discussions on AI sovereignty and how others can ensure uninterrupted access to this critical technology. For decades, many nations were comfortable having many parts of their supply chain rely on the U.S., China, and other major producers. Once a nation issues a threat, or takes action, to limit other nations’ access, other nations will rationally try to secure alternatives. For decades, semiconductor manufacturing in China made slow progress; once the U.S. moved to limit China’s access, China’s efforts kicked into high gear. Similarly, once China threatened U.S. access to rare earth minerals, U.S. efforts to secure alternatives accelerated. Now that it has become crystal clear that private U.S. companies and the U.S. government can limit, in short order, other nations’ access to frontier AI models, the incentive of others to invest more in alternatives like open source grows significantly. Of course, training frontier models is not easy, so it remains to be seen how successful they are, but we have crossed the rubicon. Satya Nadella wrote an essay about the importance of building a healthy ecosystem on top of frontier AI technology. I heartily agree with him, and hope this week’s events will ultimately prove to be constructive steps toward this. I hope we can build a more free, more open world, where research is freely shared, and laws and societal norms shape a level playing field that allows everyone to make progress. A silver lining of the events of these past two weeks is now that everyone better realizes key points of instability of the current system, we can all work to create a more stable foundation. Yes, open-source / open-weight models are important for a healthy AI ecosystem. That's how we can verify things, check claims, and keep up outside the closed labs. Plus, it gives us the freedom to run AI on our own hardware if we are not ready to share personal data and IPs with closed labs through using their models. (Not that proprietary models are bad, actually I use them a lot as well, but it wouldn't healthy not to have any alternatives.) Anyway, while pretty much everyone is waiting for the Kimi K3 and Ling 3.0 weights to land on the model hub any day now, there were quite a few other interesting new open-weight model releases the past week. Yes, one of those weeks! So, here are the architecture pics along with some notes on what I found most interesting: 1) Nanbeige 4.2 3B uses looped depth sharing. This basically means it runs the same 22-layer (=transformer block) stack twice. So, it extends the 22-layer architecture to 44-layers, but without duplicating the weights. (2x the transformer block compute but same memory footprint.) Why? The info is a bit sparse, but section 2.1 of the Nanbeige 4.2 technical report says two passes gave the best trade-off and retained about 75% of the token efficiency of a standard architecture. More passes gave barely any gains but made the training much slower and much more expensive. 2) Laguna S 2.1 is poolside's Laguna model in a really nice size: 118B sparse MoE with 8B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. Otherwise, the architecture is pretty standard. It uses 36 sliding-window and 12 global (gated-)GQA layers. However, given this size, and the fact that it (just barely) runs on my DGX Spark (uses about <80 GB of RAM), this is right now the most interesting model for me personally. It's 3x bigger and thus a tad slower but maybe a good candidate as daily-driver-Qwen3.6-35B-replacement. (Still waiting on some more independent performance benchmarks though.) 3) Motif-3-Beta is a new 314B-A13B sparse MoE that is somewhat based on DeepSeek V4 in terms of mHC and latent attention. But it uses a new component, Grouped Differential Latent Attention, which is inspired by Multi-head Latent Attention. I probably should write an article about this some time, but for now, the tl;dr is as follows. Regular MLA compresses the keys and values into a smaller latent representation to mainly reduce the KV cache size. GDLA does a similar low-rank compression but puts the attention heads into groups and also learns a noise head for each group where the noise gets subtracted for filtering purposes... Anyway, a topic for another day! 4) Solar Open 2 is a new 250B-A15B hybrid MoE by Upstage that interleaves three Kimi Delta Attention layers with one GQA layer. 5) Antares 1B is a small model (and there is also an even smaller 0.3B variant) from Cisco starts that with the IBM Granite 4.0 1B backbone and uses SFT plus GRPO for terminal-based cybersecurity stuff. It is a nice example of task-specific post-training on a genuinely small model. 6) BTL-3 is a rank-32 LoRA adapter for Qwen3.6-27B aimed at coding agents and structured tool use. The really strong benchmark performance suggests that LoRA adapters are still a useful tool/technique in 2026. I added all six to the LLM Architecture Gallery for some additional details: sebastianraschka.com/llm-arc…

The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. Overall, an exciting development! Preprint is available here ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) and will be on arxiv tonight; supporting code is here ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m

Here's the closing message I sent to everyone today. My dear friends! Today’s my last day at OpenAI. I have been thinking a lot about what I wanted to say in my final remarks to the company. Here are a few things I hope everyone takes deeply to heart. 1. For All of Humanity. What we have been building here is an opportunity to improve the human condition unlike any other in history. It’s easy to get distracted by the wealth and power that comes with this. It’s easy to focus on the already wealthy and powerful in the world, because they demand so much of our attention as customers or lawmakers or competitors. Nonetheless, do not lose sight of the “all” in “all of humanity.” Our mission for everyone. Working people. People in poverty. People who dream of a better life. What we are building can help them. It is our mission to ensure that it does. To that end, yesterday I donated a major gift to GiveDirectly, a charity that makes direct cash transfers to people in poverty in Africa and in the United States. This is a highly effective way of helping people; I encourage others to consider giving as well. 2. Risk Is Our Business. Technology changes the security equilibrium of the world profoundly and creates new risks. Some of these risks will directly result from AI; many others will result from other fields of science and engineering that are accelerated by AI. Risk is inextricable from progress. It is not a reason to turn our back on progress. I think, from time to time, of a speech from Captain Kirk in the original Star Trek—“Risk is our business,” he says about humanity as a whole. I believe this is true. But we should also be cognizant of the risks and we should actively manage them. We can simultaneously believe that it will require extraordinary effort to accomplish the safety and security of humanity, while committing to making that effort in support of our work to advance the technological frontier. The question of progress and safety is not either/or. It is definitively “both.” 3. The Consent of the Governed. OpenAI, and especially the OpenAI Foundation, will be among the most important organizations in the world. The level of power concentrated here will be like the power of a state. It demands a level of accountability that exceeds that of an ordinary company. I encourage OpenAI to pursue a path of governance innovation that makes it progressively more democratic and more beholden to the consent of the governed. All of humanity will be impacted by the work here; all of humanity should have some way to weigh in eventually. There is no roadmap for what form this should take. This is an ideal. But I hold it entirely. Thank you all again so much for being a part of an unbelievable nine year journey with me. To Safe AGI!

@MIT_CSAIL 's @a1zhang and @lateinteraction trained a model to generalize 8-32x past its training length. The research credits the harness, the scaffolding around the model, not the model itself. Train it only on short tasks, and it still handles far longer ones. That works because the harness keeps every model call close to what it was trained on. It offloads the bulk context into a code environment and keeps the results of its smaller sub-tasks out of the main chat, so the model never drowns in its own history. A few things that held up: > trains short, runs 8-32x longer > transfers across different domains > training costs 1.5-3x more Context rot, the decay your agent hits as history piles up, is often this scaffolding problem, not a weak model. highlights.text_fr: Au cours des deux dernières semaines, le gouvernement américain et Anthropic ont pris des mesures importantes qui ont démontré leur pouvoir de contrôler l'accès à l'IA en limitant ce que d'autres peuvent faire avec les modèles frontières. C'est l'un de ces moments qui, une fois vus, seront difficiles à ignorer, et cela accélère considérablement les efforts de nombreuses entreprises et nations pour assurer un accès fiable à l'IA que personne d'autre ne peut interrompre. Anthropic a d'abord publié Claude Fable 5, une version de son modèle Mythos avec des garde-fous supplémentaires, y compris certaines restrictions qui semblent bien justifiées pour des raisons de sécurité (telles que les limitations sur son application au piratage, aux armes biologiques, etc.). Cependant, il a également restreint la capacité des développeurs à l'utiliser pour construire des technologies LLM concurrentes. Cette décision était préoccupante, étant donné que toute la communauté de l'IA, y compris Anthropic, a énormément bénéficié de la recherche ouverte – en effet, la révolution de l'IA a été lancée par mon ancienne équipe (Google Brain) publiant librement l'article sur les Transformers ! Imaginez si les conditions d'utilisation de Microsoft interdisaient à quiconque d'utiliser leurs outils pour créer des logiciels concurrents, ou si Google interdisait de l'utiliser pour rechercher des informations afin de travailler sur des moteurs de recherche concurrents. L'argument d'Anthropic selon lequel il était dangereux pour d'autres de pouvoir faire des avancées en IA sonnait également faux. Initialement, Anthropic a dégradé silencieusement les performances de Fable 5 pour les utilisateurs détectés comme travaillant sur la recherche LLM par des interventions invisibles qui ont affaibli les sorties du modèle sans en informer l'utilisateur. Après des réactions négatives importantes, il est revenu sur cette décision et a décidé d'être transparent quand il le faisait, mais il refuse toujours d'utiliser ses dernières capacités pour aider les chercheurs en IA. Cette décision représente une démonstration flagrante de pouvoir de la part d'Anthropic. Il a utilisé des arguments de « sécurité » pour entraver des concurrents potentiels. Les plateformes réussissent lorsqu'elles sont considérées comme des partenaires stables et fiables sur lesquels on peut construire. Les changements soudains de règles par Anthropic (y compris une politique obligatoire de rétention des données de 30 jours pour l'utilisation de Fable) ont fait se demander aux développeurs la stabilité de la construction sur n'importe quel fournisseur de LLM propriétaire, pas seulement Anthropic. Le gouvernement américain a ensuite rapidement suivi avec une démonstration de pouvoir encore plus grande. Il a utilisé l'autorité du Département du Commerce pour réglementer les technologies qui pourraient être des menaces pour la sécurité nationale afin de restreindre les exportations de Mythos et Fable, exigeant une licence pour leur utilisation par tout ressortissant étranger, que ce soit à l'intérieur ou à l'extérieur des États-Unis, y compris les employés d'Anthropic. Cela a conduit Anthropic à désactiver l'accès à Fable pour tous les utilisateurs dans le monde. Sam Altman a souligné, en faisant référence à Anthropic, « C'est clairement un marketing incroyable de dire : 'Nous avons construit une bombe, nous sommes sur le point de la laisser tomber sur votre tête. Nous vous vendrons un abri anti-bombe pour 100 millions de dollars.' » Mais quand on s'engage dans ce type de marketing basé sur la peur, cela augmente les chances que le gouvernement américain soit d'accord avec vous et impose des contrôles à l'exportation sur la bombe que vous dites avoir construite. Pour être clair, je ne pense pas qu'Anthropic ait construit quoi que ce soit qui ressemble à une bombe, et je ne pense pas que les contrôles à l'exportation sur Fable soient appropriés. Cependant, suite à cette décision du gouvernement américain, de nombreuses nations, y compris des alliés des États-Unis, ont vu comment les États-Unis peuvent soudainement leur retirer l'accès aux modèles d'IA. Dans de nombreuses capitales du monde, cela a stimulé les discussions sur la souveraineté de l'IA et la manière dont d'autres peuvent assurer un accès ininterrompu à cette technologie critique. Pendant des décennies, de nombreuses nations se sont senties à l'aise de voir de nombreuses parties de leur chaîne d'approvisionnement dépendre des États-Unis, de la Chine et d'autres grands producteurs. Une fois qu'une nation émet une menace, ou prend des mesures, pour limiter l'accès d'autres nations, celles-ci essaieront rationnellement de trouver des alternatives. Pendant des décennies, la fabrication de semi-conducteurs en Chine a progressé lentement ; une fois que les États-Unis ont décidé de limiter l'accès de la Chine, les efforts de la Chine se sont intensifiés. De même, une fois que la Chine a menacé l'accès des États-Unis aux minéraux rares, les efforts des États-Unis pour obtenir des alternatives se sont accélérés. Maintenant qu'il est devenu clair que les entreprises privées américaines et le gouvernement américain peuvent limiter, à court terme, l'accès d'autres nations aux modèles d'IA frontières, l'incitation des autres à investir davantage dans des alternatives comme l'open source augmente considérablement. Bien sûr, l'entraînement de modèles frontières n'est pas facile, il reste donc à voir dans quelle mesure ils réussiront, mais nous avons franchi le Rubicon. Satya Nadella a écrit un essai sur l'importance de construire un écosystème sain autour de la technologie d'IA frontière. Je suis tout à fait d'accord avec lui, et j'espère que les événements de ces deux dernières semaines s'avéreront finalement être des étapes constructives dans cette direction. J'espère que nous pourrons construire un monde plus libre, plus ouvert, où la recherche est librement partagée, et où les lois et les normes sociétales créent des conditions équitables qui permettent à chacun de progresser. Une lueur d'espoir des événements de ces deux dernières semaines est que maintenant que tout le monde réalise mieux les points clés d'instabilité du système actuel, nous pouvons tous travailler à créer une base plus stable.
highlights.text_original: Over the last two weeks, both the U.S. Government and Anthropic took significant actions that demonstrated their power to control access to AI by restricting what others can do with frontier models. This has been one of those moments that, once seen, will be hard to unsee, and it is significantly accelerating many businesses’ and nation states’ efforts to ensure reliable access to AI that no one else can terminate. Anthropic first released Claude Fable 5, a version of its Mythos model with additional guardrails, including some restrictions that seem well justified on safety grounds (such as limitations on applying it to hacking, bioweapons, and so forth). However, it also restricted developers’ ability to use it to build competing LLM technology. This move was concerning, given that the whole AI community, including Anthropic, has benefitted tremendously from open research — indeed, the AI revolution was kicked off by my former team (Google Brain) freely publishing the Transformers paper! Imagine if Microsoft’s terms of use barred anyone from using their tools to build competitive software, or if Google barred using it to search for information to work on competing search engines. Anthropic’s argument that it was unsafe for others to be able to make advances in AI also rang hollow. Initially, Anthropic silently degraded Fable 5’s performance for users detected to be working on LLM research through invisible interventions that weakened the model’s outputs without notifying the user. After significant backlash, it walked back this decision and decided to be transparent when it did this, but it still refuses to use its latest capabilities to help AI researchers. This move represents a raw demonstration of power by Anthropic. It has used “safety” arguments to hinder potential competitors. Platforms succeed when they are viewed as stable, reliable partners that one can build on. The sudden rule changes by Anthropic (including a mandatory 30 day data retention policy for Fable usage) have made developers wonder about the stability of building on any one proprietary LLM provider, not just Anthropic. The U.S. Government then shortly followed with an even greater demonstration of power. It used the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate technologies that may be national security threats to restrict exports of Mythos and Fable, requiring a license for use by any foreign national, whether inside or outside of the U.S., including employees of Anthropic. This led Anthropic to disable access to Fable to all users worldwide. Sam Altman pointed out, referring to Anthropic, “It is clearly incredible marketing to say, ‘We have built a bomb, we are about to drop it on your head. We will sell you a bomb shelter for $100 million.’” But when one engages in this type of fear-based marketing, it increases the odds that the U.S. Government will agree with you and slap export controls on the bomb you say you have built. To be clear, I don't think Anthropic has built anything like a bomb, and I don't think export controls on Fable are appropriate. However, following the U.S. Government making this move, many nations, including U.S. allies, saw how the U.S. can suddenly yank their access to AI models. In many capitals around the world, this has spurred discussions on AI sovereignty and how others can ensure uninterrupted access to this critical technology. For decades, many nations were comfortable having many parts of their supply chain rely on the U.S., China, and other major producers. Once a nation issues a threat, or takes action, to limit other nations’ access, other nations will rationally try to secure alternatives. For decades, semiconductor manufacturing in China made slow progress; once the U.S. moved to limit China’s access, China’s efforts kicked into high gear. Similarly, once China threatened U.S. access to rare earth minerals, U.S. efforts to secure alternatives accelerated. Now that it has become crystal clear that private U.S. companies and the U.S. government can limit, in short order, other nations’ access to frontier AI models, the incentive of others to invest more in alternatives like open source grows significantly. Of course, training frontier models is not easy, so it remains to be seen how successful they are, but we have crossed the rubicon. Satya Nadella wrote an essay about the importance of building a healthy ecosystem on top of frontier AI technology. I heartily agree with him, and hope this week’s events will ultimately prove to be constructive steps toward this. I hope we can build a more free, more open world, where research is freely shared, and laws and societal norms shape a level playing field that allows everyone to make progress. A silver lining of the events of these past two weeks is now that everyone better realizes key points of instability of the current system, we can all work to create a more stable foundation. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

highlights.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne longue session de 'divagation'. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout est permis, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme « je passe en reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe... ». Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment très doués pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort beaucoup plus clair que ce que vous aviez au départ. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la 'fusion des esprits' et avez moins de choses à corriger par la suite.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

highlights.text_fr: Oui, les modèles open-source / open-weight sont importants pour un écosystème IA sain. C'est ainsi que nous pouvons vérifier les choses, contrôler les affirmations et nous tenir informés en dehors des laboratoires fermés. De plus, cela nous donne la liberté de faire tourner l'IA sur notre propre matériel si nous ne sommes pas prêts à partager des données personnelles et des IPs avec des laboratoires fermés en utilisant leurs modèles. (Non pas que les modèles propriétaires soient mauvais, en fait je les utilise aussi beaucoup, mais il ne serait pas sain de ne pas avoir d'alternatives.) Quoi qu'il en soit, alors que presque tout le monde attend les poids de Kimi K3 et Ling 3.0 sur le hub des modèles d'un jour à l'autre, il y a eu pas mal d'autres nouvelles sorties de modèles open-weight la semaine dernière. Oui, l'une de ces semaines ! Alors, voici les images d'architecture avec quelques notes sur ce que j'ai trouvé le plus intéressant : 1) Nanbeige 4.2 3B utilise le partage de profondeur en boucle. Cela signifie en gros qu'il exécute deux fois la même pile de 22 couches (= bloc transformateur). Il étend donc l'architecture à 22 couches à 44 couches, mais sans dupliquer les poids. (2x le calcul du bloc transformateur mais la même empreinte mémoire.) Pourquoi ? Les informations sont un peu rares, mais la section 2.1 du rapport technique de Nanbeige 4.2 indique que deux passes ont donné le meilleur compromis et ont conservé environ 75 % de l'efficacité des jetons d'une architecture standard. Plus de passes n'ont donné pratiquement aucun gain mais ont rendu l'entraînement beaucoup plus lent et beaucoup plus cher. 2) Laguna S 2.1 est le modèle Laguna de poolside dans une très belle taille : 118B MoE sparse avec 8B de paramètres actifs et une fenêtre de contexte de 1M de jetons. Sinon, l'architecture est assez standard. Il utilise 36 couches GQA (gated-GQA) à fenêtre glissante et 12 couches globales. Cependant, étant donné cette taille, et le fait qu'il fonctionne (tout juste) sur mon DGX Spark (utilise environ <80 Go de RAM), c'est en ce moment le modèle le plus intéressant pour moi personnellement. Il est 3 fois plus grand et donc un peu plus lent mais peut-être un bon candidat comme remplacement quotidien du Qwen3.6-35B. (J'attends encore des benchmarks de performance plus indépendants.) 3) Motif-3-Beta est un nouveau MoE sparse 314B-A13B qui est quelque peu basé sur DeepSeek V4 en termes de mHC et d'attention latente. Mais il utilise un nouveau composant, Grouped Differential Latent Attention, qui est inspiré de Multi-head Latent Attention. Je devrais probablement écrire un article à ce sujet un jour, mais pour l'instant, le tl;dr est le suivant. Le MLA régulier compresse les clés et les valeurs en une représentation latente plus petite pour principalement réduire la taille du cache KV. Le GDLA effectue une compression de rang inférieur similaire mais regroupe les têtes d'attention et apprend également une tête de bruit pour chaque groupe où le bruit est soustrait à des fins de filtrage... Quoi qu'il en soit, un sujet pour un autre jour ! 4) Solar Open 2 est un nouveau MoE hybride 250B-A15B par Upstage qui intercale trois couches Kimi Delta Attention avec une couche GQA. 5) Antares 1B est un petit modèle (et il existe aussi une variante encore plus petite de 0.3B) de Cisco qui commence avec le backbone IBM Granite 4.0 1B et utilise SFT plus GRPO pour les tâches de cybersécurité basées sur terminal. C'est un bel exemple de post-entraînement spécifique à une tâche sur un modèle véritablement petit. 6) BTL-3 est un adaptateur LoRA de rang 32 pour Qwen3.6-27B destiné aux agents de codage et à l'utilisation structurée d'outils. La très forte performance de référence suggère que les adaptateurs LoRA sont toujours un outil/technique utile en 2026. J'ai ajouté les six à la galerie d'architecture LLM pour plus de détails : sebastianraschka.com/llm-arc…
highlights.text_original: Yes, open-source / open-weight models are important for a healthy AI ecosystem. That's how we can verify things, check claims, and keep up outside the closed labs. Plus, it gives us the freedom to run AI on our own hardware if we are not ready to share personal data and IPs with closed labs through using their models. (Not that proprietary models are bad, actually I use them a lot as well, but it wouldn't healthy not to have any alternatives.) Anyway, while pretty much everyone is waiting for the Kimi K3 and Ling 3.0 weights to land on the model hub any day now, there were quite a few other interesting new open-weight model releases the past week. Yes, one of those weeks! So, here are the architecture pics along with some notes on what I found most interesting: 1) Nanbeige 4.2 3B uses looped depth sharing. This basically means it runs the same 22-layer (=transformer block) stack twice. So, it extends the 22-layer architecture to 44-layers, but without duplicating the weights. (2x the transformer block compute but same memory footprint.) Why? The info is a bit sparse, but section 2.1 of the Nanbeige 4.2 technical report says two passes gave the best trade-off and retained about 75% of the token efficiency of a standard architecture. More passes gave barely any gains but made the training much slower and much more expensive. 2) Laguna S 2.1 is poolside's Laguna model in a really nice size: 118B sparse MoE with 8B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. Otherwise, the architecture is pretty standard. It uses 36 sliding-window and 12 global (gated-)GQA layers. However, given this size, and the fact that it (just barely) runs on my DGX Spark (uses about <80 GB of RAM), this is right now the most interesting model for me personally. It's 3x bigger and thus a tad slower but maybe a good candidate as daily-driver-Qwen3.6-35B-replacement. (Still waiting on some more independent performance benchmarks though.) 3) Motif-3-Beta is a new 314B-A13B sparse MoE that is somewhat based on DeepSeek V4 in terms of mHC and latent attention. But it uses a new component, Grouped Differential Latent Attention, which is inspired by Multi-head Latent Attention. I probably should write an article about this some time, but for now, the tl;dr is as follows. Regular MLA compresses the keys and values into a smaller latent representation to mainly reduce the KV cache size. GDLA does a similar low-rank compression but puts the attention heads into groups and also learns a noise head for each group where the noise gets subtracted for filtering purposes... Anyway, a topic for another day! 4) Solar Open 2 is a new 250B-A15B hybrid MoE by Upstage that interleaves three Kimi Delta Attention layers with one GQA layer. 5) Antares 1B is a small model (and there is also an even smaller 0.3B variant) from Cisco starts that with the IBM Granite 4.0 1B backbone and uses SFT plus GRPO for terminal-based cybersecurity stuff. It is a nice example of task-specific post-training on a genuinely small model. 6) BTL-3 is a rank-32 LoRA adapter for Qwen3.6-27B aimed at coding agents and structured tool use. The really strong benchmark performance suggests that LoRA adapters are still a useful tool/technique in 2026. I added all six to the LLM Architecture Gallery for some additional details: sebastianraschka.com/llm-arc…

actu.text_fr: GPT-5.6 Sol Pro a résolu une question importante en statistiques. Dans le domaine des tests d'hypothèses multiples, l'objectif de contrôler le taux de fausse découverte (FDR) a été introduit dans un article séminal par Benjamini et Hochberg (1995). Ils ont également introduit une méthode (la méthode Benjamini-Hochberg ou BH) et ont prouvé qu'elle contrôlait le FDR. Cette méthode a été largement adoptée dans la science moderne à haut débit, y compris en génomique, astronomie, économie, etc. L'article a recueilli plus de 130 000 citations à ce jour. Cependant, Benjamini et Hochberg ont montré le contrôle du FDR uniquement lorsque les données pour les tests individuels sont *indépendantes*. En pratique, ces données sont souvent dépendantes ; un bon exemple est les données sur les variantes génétiques dues au déséquilibre de liaison. Des travaux ultérieurs se sont concentrés sur l'extension de la validité de la procédure BH, par exemple, à une forme de dépendance positive par Benjamini et Yekutieli (2001). La question de savoir quand la procédure BH contrôle le FDR est restée ouverte. Au cours des vingt dernières années, de nombreux auteurs, y compris Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim et van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar et Zhang (2025), ont conjecturé que la procédure BH contrôlait le FDR pour les tests bilatéraux utilisant n'importe quelles données gaussiennes corrélées. Ces auteurs ont présenté des preuves théoriques et empiriques étayant, mais ne montrant pas directement, la conjecture. Avec l'aide de l'IA (spécifiquement GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), j'ai résolu la question par la négative : La procédure Benjamini-Hochberg ne contrôle *pas* généralement le taux de fausse découverte au niveau souhaité pour les tests gaussiennes bilatéraux corrélés. Cela a été fait en présentant un modèle factoriel gaussien pour lequel, à un niveau nominal alpha=0.01, le taux de fausse découverte est prouvé être FDR>0.0104. Il y a beaucoup de commentaires intéressants à faire : 1. Ce résultat devrait intéresser tout le monde dans le domaine des statistiques. Emmanuel Candes de l'Université de Stanford a un jour qualifié le taux de fausse découverte et la procédure Benjamini-Hochberg de « l'un des deux développements les plus importants en statistiques après 1950 » (l'autre étant la régression de James-Stein). La présente conjecture est probablement la question la plus centrale concernant le FDR/BH qui était restée sans solution à ce jour. 2. GPT-5.6 a résolu le problème en une seule fois après 90 minutes de raisonnement, alors qu'avec 5.5 je n'avais pas réussi à le résoudre même après avoir itéré avec plusieurs agents parallèles pendant peut-être 20 heures. L'amélioration des capacités est donc bien réelle. Des temps passionnants à vivre ! 3. L'argument n'est pas particulièrement surprenant, mais il combine une approche asymptotique (standard pour l'analyse FDR, voir par exemple Genovese et Wasserman, Efron, etc.) avec un certificat numérique d'une manière qui serait assez non standard dans le domaine. Une fois que nous avons l'exemple spécifique, des simulations simples confirment également que le taux de fausse découverte est en effet supérieur à la valeur nominale (voir figure ci-jointe). 4. Le degré actuel de violation par rapport au niveau nominal est relativement faible (0.104 vs 0.1). L'importance de ce résultat est donc principalement conceptuelle. Les implications pratiques restent à déterminer. Globalement, un développement passionnant ! Le pré-publication est disponible ici ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) et sera sur arxiv ce soir ; le code de support est ici ( github.com/dobriban/BH ).
actu.text_original: 2023: LLMs struggle with 4th grade word problems 2024: LLMs can do high school math 2025: LLMs get a gold medal at the IMO Now, GPT-5.6 solves famous frontier math/stat questions. The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne longue session de 'divagation'. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout est permis, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme « je passe en reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe... ». Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment très doués pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort beaucoup plus clair que ce que vous aviez au départ. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la 'fusion des esprits' et avez moins de choses à corriger par la suite.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. tips.text_fr: Le « loop engineering » (ingénierie en boucle) est un mot à la mode après que des mentions de Boris Cherny (créateur de Claude Code) et Peter Steinberger (créateur d'OpenClaw) sont devenues virales sur les médias sociaux. Les boucles sont maintenant un élément clé de la façon dont nous faisons itérer les agents d'IA longuement pour construire des logiciels. Dans cette lettre, j'aimerais partager mes 3 boucles clés, présentées dans l'image ci-dessous, pour construire des produits de 0 à 1. Ces boucles guident non seulement la façon dont je construis des logiciels, mais aussi la façon dont je décide quels logiciels construire. Boucle de codage agentique : Étant donné une spécification de produit et éventuellement un ensemble d'évaluations (c'est-à-dire un ensemble de données par rapport auquel mesurer les performances), nous pouvons demander à un agent d'IA d'écrire du code, de tester son travail et de continuer à itérer jusqu'à ce que le code soit exempt de bogues et réponde à sa spécification. Cette idée de fermer la boucle a décollé vers la fin de l'année dernière, et elle a changé la donne en permettant aux agents de codage de travailler plus longtemps de manière productive sans intervention humaine. Par exemple, au cours du week-end, je construisais une application pour que ma fille pratique la dactylographie, et mon agent de codage pouvait facilement travailler pendant environ une heure, en utilisant un navigateur Web pour vérifier ce qu'il avait construit plusieurs fois avant de me revenir, sans nécessiter mon intervention. La boucle d'ingénierie s'exécute rapidement. Toutes les quelques minutes, l'agent de codage peut construire et tester une nouvelle version du logiciel. J'entends fréquemment des développeurs qui trouvent de nouvelles façons de concevoir des boucles d'ingénierie plus efficaces. C'est un domaine d'invention actif ! Boucle de rétroaction des développeurs : Dans cette boucle, un développeur examine le produit actuel et dirige l'agent de codage pour l'améliorer. L'année dernière, de nombreux développeurs (dont moi) agissaient comme la fonction QA (assurance qualité) pour nos agents de codage, trouvant manuellement les bogues puis demandant à l'agent de les corriger. Mais avec les agents de codage beaucoup plus capables de tester leur propre code, le temps que nous devons consacrer à cette fonction a considérablement diminué. Cela nous permet de prendre des décisions produit de niveau supérieur, telles que les fonctionnalités clés à offrir, où l'interface utilisateur a besoin d'améliorations, etc. La boucle de rétroaction des développeurs fonctionne sur des intervalles de temps allant de dizaines de minutes à des heures — c'est à quelle fréquence un développeur peut examiner un produit et donner des commentaires. Dans le cas de l'application de dactylographie, j'ai changé d'avis plusieurs fois sur la conception visuelle, les costumes de chat qu'elle peut débloquer en apprenant (elle adore les chats) et le flux utilisateur pour qu'un adulte se connecte et dirige l'expérience d'apprentissage de l'enfant. Lorsqu'un développeur a une vision claire de ce qu'il faut construire, il reste encore beaucoup de travail pour traduire cette vision en une spécification pour un agent de codage à implémenter. De plus, après que le développeur a vu une implémentation, il peut mettre à jour (ou peut-être clarifier) la spécification pour l'orienter vers ce qu'il veut. Si vous constatez que le système rencontre à plusieurs reprises certains problèmes, la création d'un ensemble d'évaluations pour l'agent devient utile. Les équipes natives de l'IA utilisent de plus en plus l'IA pour aider à orienter la direction du produit, par exemple, en automatisant la collecte et l'analyse des données d'utilisation, en résumant les commentaires écrits et verbaux des clients, ou en effectuant une analyse concurrentielle. Cependant, pour la plupart des produits dans lesquels je suis impliqué, je constate que les humains ont un avantage contextuel significatif sur les systèmes d'IA actuels — nous en savons beaucoup plus que le système d'IA sur les utilisateurs et le contexte dans lequel le produit doit fonctionner — et les humains jouent donc un rôle critique. Beaucoup de gens décrivent cette contribution humaine comme du « goût », mais je préfère la considérer comme les humains ayant un avantage contextuel, car cela nous donne une voie plus claire pour aider les systèmes d'IA à s'améliorer. Cela explique également pourquoi cette étape ne peut pas être automatisée : tant que l'humain sait quelque chose que l'IA ne sait pas, l'humain dans la boucle est nécessaire pour injecter cette connaissance dans le système. Boucle de rétroaction externe : Cela inclut un large éventail de tactiques comme demander l'avis à quelques amis, lancer à des testeurs alpha ou mettre le code en production avec des tests A/B. Ces tactiques sont généralement lentes, prenant rarement moins d'heures et parfois des jours, voire des semaines. Ces données informent la vision du développeur, qui à son tour continue de piloter la spécification détaillée du produit, qui à son tour pilote l'agent de codage. Avec les agents de codage accélérant le développement logiciel, de plus en plus d'ingénieurs commencent à jouer un rôle partiel de gestion de produit. Pour de nombreux ingénieurs qui évoluent vers ce rôle, la partie la plus difficile est de façonner la vision du produit et de trouver un équilibre entre la construction (combler l'écart entre la vision et la spécification) et l'obtention des commentaires des utilisateurs pour faire évoluer la vision. Il est important de faire les deux ! J'écrirai davantage sur la façon de le faire dans de futurs articles, mais pour l'instant, je trouve encourageant que les ingénieurs jouent un rôle élargi (tout comme les chefs de produit et les designers font maintenant plus d'ingénierie).
tips.text_original: “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). [Original text: The Batch]

Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late.

idees.text_fr: Voici le message de clôture que j'ai envoyé à tout le monde aujourd'hui. Mes chers amis ! Aujourd'hui est mon dernier jour chez OpenAI. J'ai beaucoup réfléchi à ce que je voulais dire dans mes remarques finales à l'entreprise. Voici quelques points que j'espère que chacun prendra profondément à cœur. 1. Pour toute l'humanité. Ce que nous avons construit ici est une opportunité d'améliorer la condition humaine sans précédent dans l'histoire. Il est facile de se laisser distraire par la richesse et le pouvoir qui en découlent. Il est facile de se concentrer sur les personnes déjà riches et puissantes dans le monde, car elles exigent tant de notre attention en tant que clients, législateurs ou concurrents. Néanmoins, ne perdez pas de vue le « toute » dans « toute l'humanité ». Notre mission est pour tout le monde. Les travailleurs. Les personnes en situation de pauvreté. Les personnes qui rêvent d'une vie meilleure. Ce que nous construisons peut les aider. Notre mission est de faire en sorte que cela se produise. À cette fin, j'ai fait hier un don important à GiveDirectly, une organisation caritative qui effectue des transferts d'argent directs aux personnes en situation de pauvreté en Afrique et aux États-Unis. C'est un moyen très efficace d'aider les gens ; j'encourage les autres à envisager de donner également. 2. Le risque est notre affaire. La technologie modifie profondément l'équilibre sécuritaire du monde et crée de nouveaux risques. Certains de ces risques résulteront directement de l'IA ; beaucoup d'autres résulteront d'autres domaines scientifiques et techniques qui sont accélérés par l'IA. Le risque est inextricable du progrès. Ce n'est pas une raison de tourner le dos au progrès. Je pense, de temps en temps, à un discours du Capitaine Kirk dans la série originale Star Trek — « Le risque est notre affaire », dit-il à propos de l'humanité dans son ensemble. Je crois que c'est vrai. Mais nous devrions également être conscients des risques et les gérer activement. Nous pouvons croire simultanément qu'il faudra des efforts extraordinaires pour assurer la sécurité de l'humanité, tout en nous engageant à faire cet effort pour soutenir notre travail visant à faire progresser la frontière technologique. La question du progrès et de la sécurité n'est pas « l'un ou l'autre ». C'est définitivement « les deux ». 3. Le consentement des gouvernés. OpenAI, et surtout la Fondation OpenAI, sera parmi les organisations les plus importantes au monde. Le niveau de pouvoir concentré ici sera comme le pouvoir d'un État. Cela exige un niveau de responsabilité qui dépasse celui d'une entreprise ordinaire. J'encourage OpenAI à poursuivre une voie d'innovation en matière de gouvernance qui la rende progressivement plus démocratique et plus redevable au consentement des gouvernés. Toute l'humanité sera impactée par le travail ici ; toute l'humanité devrait avoir un moyen d'intervenir à terme. Il n'y a pas de feuille de route pour la forme que cela devrait prendre. C'est un idéal. Mais je le maintiens entièrement. Merci encore à tous d'avoir participé à un voyage incroyable de neuf ans avec moi. Pour une AGI sûre !
idees.text_original: Here's the closing message I sent to everyone today. My dear friends! Today’s my last day at OpenAI. I have been thinking a lot about what I wanted to say in my final remarks to the company. Here are a few things I hope everyone takes deeply to heart. 1. For All of Humanity. What we have been building here is an opportunity to improve the human condition unlike any other in history. It’s easy to get distracted by the wealth and power that comes with this. It’s easy to focus on the already wealthy and powerful in the world, because they demand so much of our attention as customers or lawmakers or competitors. Nonetheless, do not lose sight of the “all” in “all of humanity.” Our mission for everyone. Working people. People in poverty. People who dream of a better life. What we are building can help them. It is our mission to ensure that it does. To that end, yesterday I donated a major gift to GiveDirectly, a charity that makes direct cash transfers to people in poverty in Africa and in the United States. This is a highly effective way of helping people; I encourage others to consider giving as well. 2. Risk Is Our Business. Technology changes the security equilibrium of the world profoundly and creates new risks. Some of these risks will directly result from AI; many others will result from other fields of science and engineering that are accelerated by AI. Risk is inextricable from progress. It is not a reason to turn our back on progress. I think, from time to time, of a speech from Captain Kirk in the original Star Trek—“Risk is our business,” he says about humanity as a whole. I believe this is true. But we should also be cognizant of the risks and we should actively manage them. We can simultaneously believe that it will require extraordinary effort to accomplish the safety and security of humanity, while committing to making that effort in support of our work to advance the technological frontier. The question of progress and safety is not either/or. It is definitively “both.” 3. The Consent of the Governed. OpenAI, and especially the OpenAI Foundation, will be among the most important organizations in the world. The level of power concentrated here will be like the power of a state. It demands a level of accountability that exceeds that of an ordinary company. I encourage OpenAI to pursue a path of governance innovation that makes it progressively more democratic and more beholden to the consent of the governed. All of humanity will be impacted by the work here; all of humanity should have some way to weigh in eventually. There is no roadmap for what form this should take. This is an ideal. But I hold it entirely. Thank you all again so much for being a part of an unbelievable nine year journey with me. To Safe AGI!

idees.text_fr: Excellents contre-arguments ici par @onlinedopamine. Les entreprises simples sont en difficulté, mais les entreprises complexes, surtout celles vendues à des sociétés IRL non-techniques, sont probablement en bonne posture. Vik (@onlinedopamine) nous vendons, entre autres, à des entreprises de services comme les hommes à tout faire, les nettoyeurs de piscines, etc. Supposer que l'une de ces personnes aura l'envie et le temps de coder un remplacement est juste une illusion. Oui, l'IA augmentera et a déjà augmenté la concurrence, mais on ne peut pas faire en sorte que les gens aient soudainement de l'initiative (nous avons récemment fait un voyage de garçons avec mon groupe d'amis de 13 gars de la maison, je suis littéralement la seule personne de ce groupe à ne pas être un employé et vous ne pourriez pas payer ces gars-là pour être des entrepreneurs). Donc, cela étant dit, je pense que ce qui est traditionnellement considéré comme un logiciel va simplement se diffuser, ce qui signifie que certains en bénéficieront énormément, comme les fournisseurs d'infrastructure comme Cloudflare, AWS, etc. (nous vendons des comptes TT réchauffés en conséquence). De même, une partie du logiciel passera du logiciel en tant que service au service en tant que logiciel (nous avons eu près de 50 clients qui nous ont demandé si nous pouvions leur fournir un service de publication de contenu ; il y a une entreprise dans notre niche et celle de Patrick appelée blaze.ai qui a absolument cartonné avec ce modèle hybride, icon.com semble également avoir été revitalisé de la même manière). (Il existe également d'autres avantages comme les données et les verrouillages, dont Salesforce bénéficie grandement par exemple). Enfin, je suis d'accord que les indépendants sont un peu foutus s'ils ne comptent que sur le référencement et les moyens traditionnels d'acquisition d'utilisateurs. Ce canal s'érode en effet (les requêtes d'information sont pratiquement mortes mais les requêtes commerciales sont toujours florissantes) et nécessite désormais d'investir de l'argent dans les backlinks (le référencement, par exemple, est un jeu à somme nulle après tout, c'est-à-dire que pour que vous gagniez un classement, quelqu'un d'autre doit le perdre). Ce que les indépendants doivent accepter, c'est le type d'entreprise qu'ils veulent vraiment construire. La plupart des produits indépendants sont un peu moyens, ce qui est logique puisque le fondateur est trop dispersé avec tout ce qu'il a à faire. Le seul vrai levier qu'ils ont, s'ils veulent un trafic et des ventes constants, est de construire une marque personnelle ou d'avoir une idée vraiment unique et d'être le premier à la commercialiser. Nous avons en fait étudié de très près le produit superscale de Patrick (et d'autres produits soutenus par du capital-risque comme creatify ou heygen) et la différence de qualité de produit par rapport à ce que les indépendants publient ici est énorme. Ce qui m'amène à mon point suivant : les indépendants doivent vraiment décider s'ils veulent continuer à faire cela seuls. Je ne pense pas que cela annonce la fin du logiciel traditionnel - des entreprises comme Canva, Veed, Figma, Notion, etc. continueront de prospérer (et je ne vois tout simplement pas l'IA, ou plutôt l'infrastructure qui l'alimente, être aussi sophistiquée au cours des 5 à 10 prochaines années pour que vous puissiez créer un produit comme Canva en une seule fois). Noah Lebovic (@NoahLebovic) I don't think it's a lack of imagination. I also used to work at Anthropic, think trends will continue, and used to agree with this. The groups I know who are using open-weight models are legitimate offensive security companies. On the inside, I know the narrative and intent is genuinely about safety. But from the outside, Anthropic-the-system seems to be optimizing for revenue and control/power, isn't diffusing capabilities to defenders, and also doesn't have adequate safeguards to prevent misuse from dedicated bad actors. As a result, I now lean towards a future where capable open models are freely available (at least for cyber, bio is harder); I don't trust Anthropic or other frontier labs to handle this sufficiently well without diffused capabilties given what I've seen so far.
